items.title: Scale Your Superpowers, Not Your Job Titles
items.summary: Luke Wroblewski's argument against using AI to do passable versions of other people's jobs: instead, take your specialised expertise — your design principles, the patterns you'd catch on review — and encode it as instructions an AI agent can apply on your behalf, so your judgment scales across more work.
items.why: A practical frame for how a design lead's taste actually travels through an org in the AI era — directly useful as you think about how CueDesign standards and your own review eye get embedded into the tools Cuemath designers and PMs are using day to day.

items.title: Apps and programming: two accidental tyrannies
items.summary: Andy Matuschak argues that two unintended constraints — the walled app as the default shape of software, and programming as a gatekept craft — have quietly suppressed interface invention for decades, and that coding agents plus composable architectures could finally let designers and domain experts shape novel interfaces directly.
items.why: Matuschak is one of the sharpest thinkers on learning tools and software's shape, and this essay puts language around something you actively wrestle with at Cuemath: what new kinds of math interfaces become possible once the cost of prototyping drops to near zero.

items.title: AI Won't Save the Kingdoms We Built
items.summary: John Cutler's argument that AI won't fix the coordination problems baked into siloed, fiefdom-shaped orgs — agents talking to agents just relocate the tax until the underlying incentives, decision rights, and team boundaries are honestly redrawn.
items.why: Product-thinking pick with an AI lens, from a writer you already trust — a useful counterweight when the conversation at work drifts to 'AI will speed us up' without asking whether the operating model is the actual bottleneck.

items.title: Make Believe
items.summary: A short note from Robin Rendle on Mac Barnett's book Make Believe: On Telling Stories to Children — arguing that good children's literature deserves real artistic seriousness, treats kids as collaborators in meaning rather than receivers of moral lessons, and trusts them with ambiguity.
items.why: A sharp reminder for kids'-product work at Cuemath: the strongest stuff for children doesn't pre-chew the meaning or hammer the lesson — it invites them in. Useful framing as you push back on overly didactic learning UX.

items.title: The Legend of Keïko / The Birth of Keïko
items.summary: A reversible book for the Keïko Tower project by Loci Anima, designed by Studio Hudson Catty: one side a novel, the other side architectural documentation, the two narratives meeting in the middle, typeset in Kalice with a butterfly-metamorphosis metaphor running through the structure.
items.why: Editorial typography fused with structural concept — the artifact itself carries the idea. A craft-level reference for the kind of editorial and brand moves you obsess over, where the format is doing as much storytelling as the type.
